newsitem.title: INDIA: India budget passage turns heat on oil prices.
newsitem.headline: India budget passage turns heat on oil prices.

text.p: Oil is the burning issue on India's economic policy agenda after the safe passage of the 1997/98 budget, with unpopular petroleum product price rises lying in wait, analysts said on Monday.

"Depoliticisation of economic policy" has become a catch phrase following the all-party support for the budget, which was passed by India's lower house last Friday and only requires rubber-stamping by the upper house.
But a decision on how to raise state-controlled oil prices is entangled in the politics of the 15-member United Front coalition.
"It is a completely political decision, and one that was very clearly required five or six months back," Tridib Pathak, analyst at UBS Securities Pvt Ltd in Bombay said.
The United Front steering committee meets on May 25, and oil prices are expected to be the main issue.
"I expect a decision within a week to 10 days, I hope it will be bold enough," said R.K. Pachouri, head of the independent Tata Energy Research Institute.

Pachouri said the situation called for a 20-25 percent increase but general speculation suggested the government will opt for a 15-20 percent increase, and may even limit rises to less for politically sensitive products like kerosene.

Kerosene is used by India's poor as their main fuel for cooking and lighting, but analysts privately estimate that more than half of the kerosene consumed is mixed illegally with gasoline for use in cars.
"It is a bit disturbing if the government limits a kerosene price hike to 10 percent as it will make adulteration of gasoline even more attactive," Pachouri said.
The United Front coalition put off raising state-controlled domestic product prices when world prices shot up six months ago, leaving oil companies to carry the extra costs.
The government needs to act quickly to remove the costly oil pool deficit, which reached 155 billion rupees ($4.33 billion) at the end of 1996/97 (April-March).

The deficit -- the money owed by the government to oil companies for selling their products below world prices -- will hit 245 billion rupees by the end of this fiscal year if nothing is done, according to junior Petroleum Minister T.R. Balu.
Meanwhile, oil companies are borrowing heavily to cover the gap, especially the Indian Oil Corp which is owed around 70-75 percent of the total deficit.
Leftist members of the 15-party coalition oppose any increase in prices, but the best they can hope for is to limit the size of the rise.

Balu wants the government to cut import and excise duties on crude oil and petroleum products by around 15 percent to alleviate the burden on oil companies and cut the deficit without raising prices too high.
Finance Minister P. Chidambaram says oil import duties cannot be cut unless other sources of government revenue are found elsewhere.

Given the number of revenue-reducing measures contained in Chidambaram's supply-side budget, it is unlikely he will want to take another with a sector that provides around 10 percent of government revenues through import and excise duties and sales taxes.
"There is a huge tussle going on between the petroleum and finance ministers," said an analyst at a foreign brokerage in Bombay.
He may end up making some concession on oil tariffs but it is unlikely to be significant, and product price hikes will be the order of the day, analysts said. ($1 = 35.8 rupees)
